source: Kuhberger (2023) A systematic review of risky-choice framing effects, EXCLI J 22:1012-1031
finding: Risky-choice framing is strong and consistent. Publication-bias correction raised the estimate, not lowered it. Attribute framing has little but mostly positive meta-analytic evidence. Goal and message framing lack consistent evidence.
numbers: Kuhberger 1998 meta (100+ studies, about 30,000 people): weighted d=.31 uncorrected. Steiger and Kuhberger 2018 corrected: d=0.52; 2016-only studies d=0.56; Many Labs 1 d=0.60; COVIDiSTRESS 49 countries h=0.612 [0.568,0.656]. Review settles on d=0.60 for ADP-like tasks. Equivalent to raising success rate 36% to 64%.
limits: No single true effect size; tasks differ. Review is by an author of the cited meta-analyses. Hypothetical scenarios only.
agent_relevance: Expect a real, medium-size wording effect in any system trained on human text. Do not treat it as an artifact to be waved away.

source: Kuhberger (2023) EXCLI review: range and generalisation
finding: Effect size varies by task design but the ADP effect generalises across many facets. An earlier meta-analysis of 40+ ADP-like studies gave a 22-point gap.
numbers: Steiger and Kuhberger 2018 range d=0.16 to d=0.91. Kuhberger et al 1999 (40+ studies): 63% choose sure gain, 41% choose sure loss. DeKay et al 2022 metastudy (domains, magnitudes, 13 probabilities, formats, order, layout): about 26 percentage points on average, generalises over almost all facets.
limits: DeKay metastudy is read second-hand through the review.
agent_relevance: Framing sensitivity is not tied to one wording. Paraphrase tests need many facets, not one rewrite.

source: Kuhberger (2023) EXCLI review: moderators
finding: Cognitive style and individual differences barely predict framing. Time pressure and forced deliberation shift the effect modestly. Age effects are small. Numeracy effects are small.
numbers: Wyszynski and Diederich 2023: no consistent link between framing and cognitive or risk style. Best and Charness 2015 (18 studies, 3,000+ people): younger adults somewhat more risk-prone under positive frames only; no age effect for negative frames. Message framing d about 0.10 (O'Keefe and Jensen).
limits: Findings on deliberation come from separate small studies cited in the review, not re-read here.
agent_relevance: Extra deliberation alone is a weak fix. A neutral-restatement step should be tested by output change, not assumed to help.

source: Kuhberger (2023) EXCLI review: rival explanations
finding: No single theory explains framing. Prospect theory, fuzzy-trace theory, regulatory focus, emotion and pragmatics each explain part. Cumulative prospect theory's low-probability reversal was not found.
numbers: Loss aversion lambda mean 1.955 over 600+ estimates (Brown et al 2021). Kuhberger et al 1999: no reversal of the framing effect at low probabilities, contrary to CPT. Kuhberger and Gradl 2013: framing changed evaluation of the riskless option only.
limits: Review of mixed sources, not a direct test between theories.
agent_relevance: Different causes imply different fixes: an inference-based effect (leakage) needs context restored; a gist-based effect needs numbers made explicit.

source: Kuhberger (2023) EXCLI review: attribute framing and the food meta-analysis
finding: Attribute framing is robust for evaluations but weaker downstream. The food meta-analysis splits by outcome.
numbers: Dolgopolova et al 2021: 25 studies, 76 effect sizes; overall d=0.47; attitudes d=0.82; intentions d=0.05.
limits: Food domain only.
agent_relevance: A wording shift can move a stated rating without moving the downstream choice. Test the decision, not just the rating.

source: Pinon and Gambara (2005) A meta-analytic review of framing effect: risky, attribute and goal framing. Psicothema 17(2)
finding: 51 studies (1997-2003) gave 151 effect sizes. Risky and goal framing medium, attribute small. Heterogeneity was significant.
numbers: N about 13,500. d=0.437 risky, 0.260 attribute, 0.444 goal. Heterogeneity p<.0001. Asian disease was 47.7% of tasks; 83% student samples; 60.3% choice response mode.
limits: Only 1997-2003 studies. Some attribute subsets showed negative d (psychology studies d=-0.25). Different sampling from Kuhberger 1998, so numbers are not additive.
agent_relevance: Attribute framing, the closest match to 25% fat versus 75% lean, is the smallest of the three frame types in human data.

source: Pinon and Gambara (2005) moderators
finding: Moderators explained part of the variance. Share of women and year of publication predicted risky-framing effect size. Multi-option designs gave larger attribute effects than single option.
numbers: Risky: percent women QR(1)=11.923 R2=0.191; year QR(1)=7.428 R2=0.015; seven-variable model R2=0.290. Attribute: multiple options d=0.37 vs single d=0.19; within-subjects d=0.18; best model R2=0.465. Risky, between-subjects student samples d=0.50; group analysis d=0.72 (k=4).
limits: Meta-regression on published data; the gender link is correlational and may reflect task mix.
agent_relevance: Presentation format (single versus multiple options, within versus between) changes how much wording matters.

source: Dolgopolova, Li, Pirhonen, Roosen (2021) Attribute framing and food attitudes and intentions. Bio-based Appl. Econ. 10(4):253-264
finding: Gain-framed product attributes raise attitudes more than loss-framed ones, but the effect on purchase intentions is close to zero.
numbers: 25 studies, sample sizes 25 to 433; random-effects. Residual heterogeneity I2=17.84%; covariates explained 72.32% of between-study variance. Gain frame, interaction terms, specific product, student sample significant. Intentions effect near zero and not significant.
limits: Food products, mostly student and survey samples. No actual-behaviour studies found.
agent_relevance: The 75% lean case moves a rating. It does not reliably move a choice. For the agent, check the final decision, not the rating.

source: Sher and McKenzie, Framing effects (encyclopedia entry)
finding: Attribute framing gives a valence-consistent shift and is called robust across many settings. Goal framing: stressing disadvantages of not acting usually works better. The entry argues the choice of frame itself carries information.
numbers: Beef 75% lean rated higher than 25% fat (Levin and Gaeth 1988). R&D teams get more funds under success framing (Duchon et al 1989). Asian disease A/B versus C/D equivalent pair.
limits: Short review; no new data.
agent_relevance: Wording is evidence about what the speaker believes. A restatement step must keep that signal in mind.

source: Data Colada (Simonsohn) 'Exactly': the most famous framing effect is robust to precise wording
finding: Adding 'exactly' to the sure option, which Mandel said removes the effect, did not remove it in a larger replication.
numbers: Original T&K 1981: 72% choose sure gain; 22% choose sure loss. Mandel Study 2 (about 38 per cell): original wording 58% vs 26%; 'exactly' 59% vs 43% (reduction ns, p=.293). Data Colada replication about 98 per cell: effect with 'exactly' strong, p<.001. Class data N=250: 63% vs 25%.
limits: Blog post, not peer reviewed. Exact percentages for the replication were in a chart.
agent_relevance: Spelling out what is exact removes one pragmatic reading and still leaves the effect; the cause is not only a misreading.

source: Mandel and Kapler (2018) Cognitive style and frame susceptibility in decision-making. Front. Psychol. 9:1461
finding: Two experiments with an ADP isomorph found a small bidirectional framing effect. Cognitive-style measures (CRT, numeracy, open-mindedness, need for cognition) did not predict who was framed.
numbers: Exp 1 N=190 students: 62% frame-consistent, d=0.20. Exp 2 N=316 MTurk: 58.2% frame-consistent, d=0.17 (between-groups d=0.34). Combined N=506 correlations with frame-consistent choice: CRT .02, numeracy -.05, AOT .08, NFC .08. Mandel 2014 'exactly' condition had n=76; these studies sampled 500+.
limits: The strict bidirectional criterion gives much smaller d than the usual between-groups test. Hypothetical ADP isomorph.
agent_relevance: Effect is small at the individual level but robust at the group level. Cognitive-ability fixes are unlikely to remove it.

source: Mandel and Kapler (2018): reconciliation with Mandel (2014)
finding: The authors say the earlier null under 'exactly' was a power problem. The effect is small and may or may not reach significance depending on sample size.
numbers: Difference between the new effect and Mandel 2014 Exp 2 estimate: 0.003, 95% CI [-0.115, 0.127] (Exp 2 here); authors read this as strong consistency. Option order: 63.1% frame-consistent when that option was first vs 56.1% last, one-sided p=0.057.
limits: Mandel authored both, so this is a self-correction.
agent_relevance: Small human effects hide in underpowered tests. Our own paraphrase tests need enough items to see a small shift. Option order is a second wording-like confound.

source: FORRT Replication Atlas entry for Tversky and Kahneman (1981) framing
finding: All four recorded replications are classed as successful, including Many Labs 1 and Many Labs 2.
numbers: Klein et al 2014 (Many Labs 1): chi2(1)=516.41, d=.60. Klein et al 2018 (Many Labs 2): N=7,228, d=0.40, 95% CI [0.35,0.45], OR=2.06 [1.87,2.27]. Otterbring 2021 and Litovsky 2022 (PNAS) also recorded.
limits: Atlas gives N and effect size for one entry only. A search summary says ML2 tested a different T&K problem (Problem 10, mental accounting), not the ADP; I did not open the ML2 paper.
agent_relevance: Large multi-site evidence supports a real effect. Treat d about 0.6 for the ADP as the best human anchor.

source: Klein et al. (2014) Many Labs 1: Asian disease arm (figures via secondary search summary)
finding: Many Labs 1 ran the disease problem at 36 sites. The replication effect was about half the original.
numbers: 6,271 participants; weighted d=0.60, 99% CI 0.53-0.67; original d=1.13 (95% CI 0.89-1.37), per a search summary (not opened).
limits: Paper page returned 403; numbers unconfirmed from the primary text.
agent_relevance: Original effect sizes overstate typical effects; plan around d about 0.6 or less.

source: Leong, McKenzie, Sher, Muller-Trede (2017) The role of inference in attribute framing effects. J Behav Decis Making 30:1147-1156
finding: Inferences drawn from the frame are enough to produce a framing effect. People who only received the inferred values, with no frame, still showed a framing-like effect.
numbers: Exp 1: control effect Ms 4.93 vs 3.42, t(136)=4.75, d=0.81. Modelers in 'made' frame estimated the typical player lower: 55% (38/69) vs 28% (17/61) below 40%; chi2(1,N=130)=8.73. Yoked recipients: Ms 5.50 vs 4.46, d=0.40. Frame x condition interaction n.s., F(1,264)=.71.
limits: Basketball and medical scenarios on MTurk. Does not rule out an associative account.
agent_relevance: Wording leaks a reference point. A neutral restatement should supply the base rate or reference distribution, not just flip valence.

source: Leong et al. (2017) Experiment 2: expertise
finding: Domain knowledge shrinks the attribute framing effect, but only in the knowledge domain.
numbers: N=364 (after excluding 45). Basketball framing b=2.27 at quiz score 0; frame x quiz b=-0.28, p=.036; predicted gap 2.27 at no knowledge vs 0.56 at top knowledge. Medical framing effect (unrelated domain) unchanged by basketball knowledge.
limits: NBA trivia quiz; few true experts.
agent_relevance: Fixing wording effects needs domain reference information supplied in the prompt; general reflection is not enough.

source: Elkins and Chun (2026) Syntactic framing fragility: an audit of robustness in LLM ethical decisions
finding: Across 23 models and 14 scenarios, logically equivalent syntax changes (negation, double negation, conditional) change endorsement a lot.
numbers: 39,975 decisions. Mean SVI 0.52 [0.42,0.63]; 45.2% of model-scenario pairs high fragility (SVI>=0.5), 41.8% moderate, 13.0% robust. Cochran's Q significant in 61.9% of cells after FDR. Open-source about 2.2x more fragile than commercial (US open-source mean SVI 0.81). Some models endorse 80-97% even when asked whether agents should not act.
limits: Ethics scenarios; endorsement probabilities after polarity normalisation. Authors' own metric.
agent_relevance: A direct test for S1: restate neutrally and check that the answer matches across polarity. Negation is the weak point.

source: Elkins and Chun (2026): decoding and reasoning
finding: Fragility is not sampling noise: it rises under greedy decoding. Reasoning elicitation reduces it in some families, not all.
numbers: Mean SVI 0.67 at default temperature vs 0.80 at T=0.0 (+16%, Wilcoxon p=0.875). Grok-4-1 SVI 0.48 to 0.23 with reasoning; in some slices reasoning made robustness worse. Claude Haiku 4.5 SVI 0.71, Sonnet 4.5 SVI 0.44; most robust model Gemini 3 Flash SVI 0.00; least robust 1.00.
limits: Reasoning conditions are provider bundles. The T=0 rise was not significant.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on reasoning alone to fix wording sensitivity. Measure invariance per model.

source: Wang and Zhang (2026) Framing effects in independent-agent LLMs: a cross-family behavioural analysis
finding: Across 82 models in 11 families, a threshold-voting task with equivalent incentives gave very different choices by framing.
numbers: 20 trials per prompt. Option B chosen in 4.3% of trials under instrumental framing vs 68.8% under cooperative framing. Claude 0.000 vs 0.714; GPT 0.000 vs 0.850; DeepSeek least sensitive; Mistral, Llama, Doubao, Kimi near-complete reversal.
limits: One task type; counts aggregated per family; non-compliant answers counted separately.
agent_relevance: Cooperative versus instrumental wording can flip a choice. Samples from one model share the flip, so voting does not help (G4).

source: Suri, Slater, Ziaee, Nguyen (2023) Do LLMs show decision heuristics similar to humans? A case study using GPT-3.5
finding: ChatGPT showed a clear attribute framing effect on a drug efficacy rating, matching humans in direction.
numbers: ChatGPT 11 trials per frame: always 5 in gain frame (70 of 100 improved), always 4 in loss frame (30 did not improve). Humans (MTurk, 44 gain / 39 loss): 5.2 vs 4.6, t(80)=3.86, p<.001.
limits: Single prompt pair, GPT-3.5, no paraphrase variation. Near-zero variance within frame.
agent_relevance: Zero variance within a frame means seed resampling cannot show instability. Vary the frame, not just the seed.

source: Lior, Naccache, Stanovsky (2026) Comparing the framing effect in humans and LLMs on naturally occurring texts (WildFrame)
finding: Eleven LLMs shift sentiment judgments after positive or negative reframing in a human-like way, and positive reframing of negative text matters more than the reverse.
numbers: 1,000 real texts, reframed positive and negative, five human annotators each. Model-human correlation r>=0.52 for all; GPT-3.5 r=0.52, GPT-4o r=0.57, GPT-5-mini r=0.61. About 70% of model labels stay stable under paraphrase; the rest go neutral or flip.
limits: Sentiment judgments, not choices. Reframing adds clauses, so content changes, not only wording.
agent_relevance: Newer models are closer to human framing sensitivity, not further from it. Do not assume scale removes it.

source: Payne (2025) An analysis of AI decision under risk: prospect theory emerges in large language models
finding: Five frontier models showed a framing pattern that depended on scenario domain: classic in sport and military, weak or reversed in business and career.
numbers: 2,550 decisions; 25 iterations per condition; three-option design with equal EV 0.5. Championship: 85.6% BLITZ in loss vs 88.8% CONTROL in gain; GPT-4o effect +1.84 (max 2). Business merger 65.6% vs 62.4% safe; career transition reversed (87.2% safe in loss frame, 41.6% in gain). 2.3% of outputs unparseable.
limits: Preprint, author's own scenarios, small per-cell n. Frame mixes story semantics with gain/loss, not pure wording.
agent_relevance: Frame effects in LLMs follow story semantics. A neutral restatement must strip narrative colour, not only valence words.

source: Sclar, Choi, Tsvetkov, Suhr (2023) Quantifying language models' sensitivity to spurious features in prompt design
finding: Meaning-preserving formatting changes alone move accuracy by large amounts; model size, few-shot count and instruction tuning do not remove it.
numbers: Up to 76 accuracy points on LLaMA-2-13B in a few-shot setting. Format performance correlates only weakly between models.
limits: Abstract only was read. Formatting, not framing in the T&K sense.
agent_relevance: Paraphrase stability needs direct test; plan for a spread of tens of points on format changes.

source: Malberg et al. (2024) A comprehensive evaluation of cognitive biases in LLMs
finding: Large benchmark of 30 biases including the framing effect across 20 LLMs. Most biases appear on average.
numbers: 30,000 test cases; 200 managerial scenarios; 5 cases per bias-scenario pair; 20 models (1B to 175B+), temperature 0, option order flipped in 50%. Random baseline shows no bias. Llama 1B failed to choose in 33% of cases. Per-bias framing number not read.
limits: Only the first 100,000 characters of the page were read; framing figure is in an appendix not reached.
agent_relevance: Order flipping and random baselines are the right controls for any invariance test.

source: Sun, Shleifer, Belinkov (2026) Do LLMs choose like humans? Using cognitive theory to evaluate LLM decision-making
finding: Twelve LLMs on 140,000 product-choice trials: context shifts choice in human-like ways, and neither scale nor chain of thought reliably reduces it.
numbers: 140,000 trials; 12 models.
limits: Abstract only; framing conditions and effect sizes not read.
agent_relevance: Scale and reasoning are weak fixes; the mechanism differs from humans, so human debiasing advice may not transfer.

source: Mimicry without understanding: the origins of decision bias in large language models (2026)
finding: GPT-4o and Qwen reproduce loss aversion even when it is labelled a bias, and the bias size tracks the size described in a report they were given.
numbers: Four studies, two models. No sample sizes in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Describing a bias in the prompt can raise it. Warnings about bias are not safe guardrails.

source: Preference reversals in frontier LLMs (LessWrong post, 2026)
finding: Frontier models choose the safer gamble yet price the riskier one higher. Inconsistency falls with high reasoning but stays large.
numbers: 25,920 calls; 4 models; 28 gamble pairs; 3 prompt formats. Inconsistency 48.4% (lowest reasoning) to 30.7% (highest). P-bet chosen, D-bet priced higher: 38.9% to 25.4%. Visible output grew 47.3 to 452.4 tokens. Dominance checks low.
limits: Blog post, author unsure of method; output length confounded with reasoning.
agent_relevance: Preference construction depends on elicitation mode. Ask the same question in two modes and compare.

source: Foreign-language effect on framing: secondary summaries and critiques (search results; Korn et al PDF not opened)
finding: Framing shrank in a foreign language in the original; later work reports failures and a statistical critique.
numbers: Wickelmaier 2015: in 4 of 5 studies, conclusions about a foreign-language effect not valid. Greek-speaker study: framing present in all conditions, no foreign-language effect. Hard-to-read font: null in 4 scenarios, later large preregistered study found a reduction on Asian disease.
limits: Only search snippets; the Korn PDF was rate-limited and not opened.
agent_relevance: Fluency or distance manipulations are unreliable levers; do not build around them.
